idiom_name: JVM JCA via java.security/javax.crypto: Cipher, SecureRandom, KeyStore
implementation_notes: Scala has no cryptography of its own - scala.util.Random is a convenience generator on top of java.util.Random, not a security API - so the mechanism is the JVM platform: the JCA's named algorithms, secure random and keystore. The Scala realization is a thin, explicit wrapper: Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding") and SecureRandom behind a typed boundary (an ADT of permitted algorithms instead of a string passed around; a Resource/ZIO service that scopes a key's lifetime), while keys live in a KeyStore or KMS. The functional packaging is idiomatic, not a substitute for the public primitive; a hand-rolled cipher or a key compiled into an object is the inversion.
code_sketch:
val key: SecretKey = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12").getKey(alias, pw)   // secret
val rng = SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong()
val iv = { val b = new Array[Byte](12); rng.nextBytes(b); b }            // nonce
val c = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")                         // public alg
c.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, new GCMParameterSpec(128, iv))
val ct = c.doFinal(plaintext)
pitfalls: scala.util.Random (including Random.nextBytes) is not cryptographically secure; keys and nonces come from SecureRandom, scoped like any other effect/resource.
Algorithm strings are resolved by the runtime provider, so an untyped "AES" or a legacy mode can silently select a different implementation; name the full transform and assert it in tests.
Secrets in application.conf or an object's val are committed or compiled: use the keystore/KMS and resolve configuration at runtime, never the default example secret that ships with the config.
